How do you build a city eighty-five metres down, into solid rock, with nothing but hand tools?
And why would anyone want to?
Beneath an ordinary town in central Turkey there is a second town.
It was not built.
It was dug, straight down into the rock, level below level.
It had stables, kitchens, wine presses, wells and a church, and doors of solid stone that could be rolled shut from the inside.
This is Derinkuyu.
In this film we answer three questions: how it was built, who built it, and why people would choose to live underground.
For centuries the town above had almost forgotten it.
Then, in 1963, a man renovating his house knocked through a wall and found a passage behind it.
The passage led to another, and that one led down.
What the people of Derinkuyu uncovered over the following years was one of the largest underground settlements ever found.
It was not alone.
Across the region of Cappadocia, dozens of other underground settlements have been found, some small, some huge, a few joined, perhaps, by tunnels.
Together they are among the strangest things that people have ever made: whole villages that could vanish into the ground.
But almost everything you may have heard about it needs checking.
That it has eighteen levels.
That twenty thousand people lived in it.
That a Greek soldier described it two and a half thousand years ago.
Some of this is true, some is exaggerated, and some is simply wrong.
Let us go down and see what the evidence actually says.
To understand Derinkuyu you have to start with the ground it was cut from.
Cappadocia lies on the high plateau of central Anatolia.
Millions of years ago, volcanoes such as Erciyes and Hasan buried this landscape under thick layers of ash.
Pressed and settled over time, the ash became a pale, soft rock called tuff.
The volcanoes were not only ancient history.
Mount Hasan, west of Derinkuyu, erupted within the time of human memory.

Geologists who dated its youngest rocks found an eruption about nine thousand years ago, and some archaeologists think a wall painting at Çatalhöyük, a Neolithic town on the Konya plain, shows a twin-peaked volcano erupting above a settlement.
Whether the painting really shows Hasan is still debated.
But the people of this region have lived beside volcanoes for as long as there have been people here.
Wind and water carved the tuff into the strange cones and pillars that make Cappadocia famous today, the so-called fairy chimneys.
Where a harder cap of rock protected the softer tuff below, a tall pillar was left standing as the land around it wore away.
The same softness made it easy to dig.
With iron tools a person can cut tuff almost like hard clay, yet a room carved in it will stand for centuries.
So for thousands of years the people of Cappadocia did not only build upward.
They dug in.
They cut houses, pigeon houses, storerooms and churches into the cliffs and the cones.
Carving had another advantage.
A carved room needs no timber for its roof, and timber was scarce on this treeless plateau.
It needs no mortar and no bricks.
And it stays cool in summer and holds its warmth in winter.
For poor farmers, a room cut into the rock was cheaper and more comfortable than one built on top of it.
Underground settlements were the next step down.
Dozens of them have been recorded across the region, and new ones are still being found.
Most are small.
A few are enormous.
The two largest open to visitors lie only a few kilometres apart, at Kaymaklı and here at Derinkuyu.
Today these valleys are protected together with the rock churches of Göreme.
UNESCO listed them as a World Heritage Site in 1985, under the name Göreme National Park and the Rock Sites of Cappadocia.
Derinkuyu is one of the sites named in that listing.
The fairy chimneys are beautiful, but they are also a warning.
The same softness that let people carve the rock lets wind, rain and frost carve it too.
Every winter, water seeps into cracks, freezes and pushes the rock apart.
Every spring, the meltwater carries the loosened grains away.
A chimney survives as long as its cap.
The cap is a block of harder rock, often a layer of more resistant volcanic material, that shields the soft tuff beneath it from the rain.
When the cap finally falls, the cone below begins to wear down quickly, and in time it disappears.
People have had to live with this.
At Zelve, a valley full of carved houses and churches, families lived in the rock until the middle of the twentieth century.
In the 1950s the danger of collapse became too great, and the inhabitants were moved to a new village nearby.
Zelve is now an open-air museum of empty rooms.
Not every carved hill was so fragile.
At Uçhisar, a great crag of tuff rises over the surrounding valleys, honeycombed with rooms and passages.
It was a natural fortress, a lookout over the whole region, and from its top on a clear day you can see Mount Erciyes far to the east.
Underground, the rock is protected from all of this.
There is no frost, no rain and no wind below the first few metres.
That is one reason the underground cities have survived better than many of the carved houses above.
Their enemy is not the weather but water seeping through the rock, and the slow weight of the ground overhead.
So how do you build a city by digging down?
Start with what the builders had.
They had a rock that is soft when fresh, and which a person can cut with hand tools.
They had iron picks and adzes.
They had oil lamps, baskets and rope.
And they had time: not years, but generations.
That turns out to be enough.
How was it dug?
Not with machines, and not with anything exotic.
The walls still carry the marks of the tools: the short strokes of picks and adzes, the kind of iron tools a farmer or a stonemason in Cappadocia would have owned.
A digger worked forward into the face of the rock, by the light of an oil lamp, loosening the tuff in small pieces.
Every basket of loose rock then had to be carried out, up the passages and stairs, to the surface.
Nobody knows where all of it went.
It may have been spread on the fields, used as building material, or simply dumped in the valleys.
For a city this size, the amount of rock removed is enormous.
That is one reason most researchers think it was the work of many generations, not of one.
A city like this is not dug all at once.
It probably started with a few rooms, perhaps cellars under houses, reached by short passages.
When that room is not enough, the diggers cut another beside it, or a stair leading down to a new room below.
Each new level is reached from the one above.
Over the generations, a few rooms become a level, and the levels become a city.
Why has it lasted?
Tuff is weak compared with granite or limestone.
A space cut into it stays up only if its span is modest and enough solid rock is left around it.
That is what the builders did.
They kept most rooms small, left thick walls and pillars of rock between them, and did not stack every room directly on top of the one below.
The vertical shafts were part of the plan from early on.
A level cut deep under the ground is useless if no air reaches it, so shafts had to be dug down from the surface, or up from below, to carry fresh air and to reach water.
We will come back to how well that system worked.
And the famous rolling stone doors were cut on the spot, from the rock of the city itself, because they could never have been carried down those narrow passages.
So the answer to the first question is simpler than the legends and, in its way, more impressive.

Derinkuyu was built by hand, with ordinary iron tools, by lamplight, by people who understood one kind of rock better than almost anyone has before or since, working room by room over many generations.
What we cannot say is exactly when it began, how long it took, or how many hands it needed.
No record of the work survives, and anyone who gives you precise numbers is guessing.
Long before anyone dug Derinkuyu, Cappadocia was already one of the busiest places in the ancient world.
Nearly a hundred kilometres north-east of Derinkuyu, near the modern city of Kayseri, stands a great mound called Kültepe.
Under it lie the ruins of a city that its own people called Kanesh.
Nearly four thousand years ago, in the twentieth and nineteenth centuries before Christ, merchants from the city of Assur, in what is now northern Iraq, settled at Kanesh.
They lived in their own quarter at the foot of the citadel, the karum, or harbour, although there was no sea.
Donkey caravans brought them tin and fine woollen cloth from Mesopotamia, which they sold for silver and gold.
We know this in astonishing detail because the merchants wrote everything down.

More than twenty thousand clay tablets have been excavated at Kültepe: letters between business partners, contracts, loans, lawsuits, and letters from wives in Assur complaining that the money had not arrived.
They are written in Old Assyrian, in cuneiform, and they form one of the oldest large archives of private letters ever found.
The letters are often startlingly human.
Merchants complain about prices and taxes, worry about smugglers on the road, and argue with their partners.
Women in Assur ran the weaving side of the business and wrote to their husbands and brothers in Kanesh, sometimes sharply, about money they were owed.
Some merchants married local women in Anatolia, and their contracts survive too.
The tablets also preserve something else: the names of the local people.
Many of them are in an Indo-European language, the earliest trace of the language we call Hittite.
Later the Hittites themselves would call their own tongue nesili, the language of Nesa, which was another name for Kanesh.
In a sense, the written history of Anatolia begins here, in Cappadocia.
The Hittite kingdom that followed ruled central Anatolia for centuries, from its capital at Hattusa, north-west of Cappadocia.
It fought Egypt at the battle of Kadesh and signed one of the earliest peace treaties that survives.
When it collapsed, around 1200 BC, the region broke into smaller kingdoms, and for a while the written record grows thin.
None of this tells us when Derinkuyu was begun.
No tablet mentions an underground city, and nothing found in Derinkuyu has been dated to the Bronze Age.
But it shows what kind of land this was: rich, crossed by trade routes, and worth fighting over.
A land like that would always need places to hide.
The name Cappadocia first appears in writing in the inscriptions of the Persian king Darius the Great, around 520 BC, as Katpatuka, one of the lands of his empire.
You will often read that the name means the land of beautiful horses.
It is a lovely story, but its origin is really unknown.
What is certain is that Cappadocian horses were famous.
The geographer Strabo says the province once paid the Persian king a yearly tribute that included fifteen hundred horses.
The Persian empire fell to Alexander the Great in the 330s BC, but Cappadocia was never fully conquered by him.
After his death, a local dynasty took the title of king.
The kings of Cappadocia ruled from the city of Mazaca, at the foot of Mount Erciyes, and minted silver coins with their portraits.
Squeezed between larger powers, the kings of Cappadocia learned to survive by choosing their friends carefully.
In the end they became clients of Rome.
The last king, Archelaus, renamed Mazaca Caesarea in honour of the emperor Augustus, and in the year 17 AD the emperor Tiberius made Cappadocia a Roman province.
Rome's interest was not only strategic.
Cappadocia was a land of great estates, horses and flocks, and of temple-states where whole territories belonged to a god and were run by his priests.
The most famous was Comana, whose temple of the goddess Ma, Strabo says, had thousands of temple servants.
It was a very different world from the cities of the Aegean coast.
Under Rome, the great roads to the eastern frontier ran across the plateau, and Caesarea grew into one of the important cities of Asia Minor.
Soldiers and supplies moved east along these roads.
So, in later centuries, would invaders moving west.
Christianity arrived early.
When the New Testament describes the crowd in Jerusalem at Pentecost, Cappadocians are named among them.
The First Letter of Peter is addressed to Christians scattered across Asia Minor, Cappadocia among them.
By the fourth century, Caesarea was one of the great centres of the Christian world.
It is in this Christian Cappadocia that the underground cities first come clearly into view.
But before we follow that story, let us go back down into Derinkuyu and see the city itself, level by level.
From the street, almost nothing shows.
The entrance is a low doorway in a modest building in the middle of town.
Inside, a passage slopes down, so narrow and low in places that visitors have to stoop and walk in single file.
That was not an accident.
A narrow passage is easy to defend.
The first levels are the busiest.
Here are the rooms people needed every day: stables for animals near the surface, wide halls, kitchens blackened by smoke, storerooms and niches for lamps.
Basins cut into the floor are usually read as wine or oil presses, though no one can say exactly what was pressed in each.
Below them the city keeps going.
Stairs and ramps lead from one level to the next, and every one is a little cooler and darker than the last.
At least eight levels are known, reaching about eighty-five metres below the surface.
Only part of the complex is open to visitors, and some of it has never been fully cleared.
Deep down is a long room with a vaulted ceiling, often called the missionary school, though the name is a modern guess.
Lower still is a cross-shaped church cut into the rock.
A church this deep tells us something important about the people who used the city at a later stage of its history: they were Christians.
Moving between levels was deliberately awkward.
Stairs turn, passages narrow, and in places a visitor must crouch to pass.
An attacker coming down would have to do so one at a time, bent over, in the dark, while the defenders waited on the far side of a stone door.
The architecture itself was a weapon.
How long people stayed underground at any one time is not recorded.
Most experts think the city was not a permanent home but a refuge, filled when danger came and emptied when it passed.
Families would have brought their animals, their grain and their oil, closed the doors behind them, and waited.
A city eighty-five metres underground has two problems that matter more than anything else.
People need to breathe, and they need to drink.
Derinkuyu solved both with the same idea: vertical shafts cut straight down through the rock.
Some shafts run from the surface down through the levels, bringing fresh air to every floor.
Air moves through them because the underground stays at much the same cool temperature all year while the air outside changes, so the difference pushes air in and out.
The system still works: even on the lowest levels open to visitors, the air is fresh enough to breathe without difficulty.
Other shafts were wells.
They were dug down to the groundwater, and the deepest is reported to reach about fifty-five metres.
A well that could be reached from inside the city meant that people sheltering below did not have to go up for water, the most dangerous moment of any siege.
Water also posed a danger.
Rain seeping down through cracks could soften the tuff, and a flooded passage could cut a level off.
Water still finds its way down today; in some rooms it trickles quietly over the walls.
Keeping the city dry was a task that never ended.
None of this needed advanced technology.
It needed patience, experience and a very good understanding of this one kind of rock.
The people who dug Derinkuyu learned what tuff would and would not do, probably over many generations, and passed that knowledge on.
What was it like to shelter here?
No one who did so left us a description, so we have to read the rooms themselves, and be honest about where the evidence stops.
The first thing to understand is the darkness.
Below the first levels no daylight reaches at all.
Every task, cooking, feeding animals, caring for the sick, was done by the light of small oil lamps, and the niches cut for them can still be seen in the walls, often with soot on the rock above.
Lamps burn oil and use up air, which is one more reason the ventilation mattered so much.
The second is the cold.
The underground keeps a cool, steady temperature, which is excellent for storing food and wine, and miserable for sitting still for days.
People would have brought blankets and bedding down with them, along with grain, oil, dried food and water jars.
The many storerooms and niches show how much of the city was simply a larder.
The third is the animals.
The stables near the top were not decoration.
A family that left its sheep, goats and draught animals above ground would lose them to the raiders, and with them its future.
So the animals came down too, which means the smell, the noise and the waste of the animals came too.
How long could people stay?
The honest answer is that we do not know.
With stored food and a well, a community could in principle hold out for weeks.
Most raids, though, were measured in days.
The point of the city was not to live below for ever.
It was to outlast the danger and come back up to fields and houses that were still there.
The most famous objects in Derinkuyu are its doors.
They are not doors in the ordinary sense.
They are great discs of stone, shaped like millstones, standing on edge in a slot beside the passage.
When danger came, the people inside rolled the stone across the opening and sealed it.
Look closely at how they sit and you see the logic.
The slot is on the inside.
The stone could be moved only from the city's side, and once it was in place there was nothing on the outside for an attacker to grip.
Each level could be closed separately, so if one level fell, the people below could still shut themselves in.
Some descriptions add that the doors had a hole in the centre, through which defenders could thrust a spear at anyone outside.
Several of the stones do have central holes, but what they were for is not certain.
They may simply have helped people move the stones.
Kaymaklı and Özkonak have the same kind of doors, cut and placed in the same way.
That suggests a shared tradition, a way of building that spread from village to village across the region.
Whoever designed the first one, it worked well enough to be copied again and again.
How heavy were they?
You will find figures from two hundred kilograms to a thousand.
None of them comes from a published survey, so we will not give one.

What is certain is that they were heavy enough to need several people to roll, and that they were cut from the same rock as the city, on the spot, because they could never have been brought down the narrow passages.
Narrow passages, low ceilings, sharp turns and doors that close from the inside: everything about Derinkuyu says the same thing.
It was built by people who expected to be attacked, and who knew they could not win a fight in the open.
Their answer was to make themselves impossible to reach.
So who were they?
This is the hardest question about Derinkuyu, and the honest answer is that no one knows who cut the first chamber.
There is no inscription at the entrance and no founder's name.
Carved rooms are very hard to date, because rock has no layers that build up over time the way a mound of earth does.
You will often read that it was begun by the Phrygians, a people of Anatolia in the eighth and seventh centuries before Christ.
Some scholars have suggested this, and Phrygians did cut rock monuments elsewhere in Anatolia.
But there is no direct evidence linking them to Derinkuyu.
It is a possibility, not a fact.
Another favourite claim is that the Greek writer Xenophon described Derinkuyu.

Around 400 BC he marched across Anatolia with an army of Greek mercenaries, and in his book, the Anabasis, he describes villages whose houses were dug into the ground, entered through a narrow opening like the mouth of a well and wide inside, with ramps for the animals and ladders for the people.
But read where he says it.
Xenophon was describing villages in Armenia, in the mountains of eastern Anatolia, hundreds of kilometres from Cappadocia.
His houses were real, and they show that living underground was an old idea in Anatolia.
They are not Derinkuyu.
Others have pointed to the Hittites, or to people even older.
Again there is no evidence.
The Hittites did build underground passages, such as the long stone tunnel under the walls of Hattusa, but those were built of masonry, not cut into soft rock, and they are a long way from Derinkuyu.
Most researchers think the city grew in stages.
The upper levels and the lower ones are not necessarily the same age, and rooms were widened, joined and dug deeper over many centuries.
Derinkuyu was not built.
It accumulated.
Archaeologists usually date a site by digging down through layers.
The deeper the layer, the older it is, and the pottery, coins and bones in each layer give it a date.
An underground city turns this upside down.
It was made by taking rock away, not by building anything up, and the empty rooms carry no layers of their own.
Worse, the rooms were used for centuries and cleared out many times.
Whatever the first users left behind was swept away by the next ones, and much of what remained was removed again when the city was cleared for visitors in the 1960s.
So the objects found inside tell us mostly about the last people to use it.
What researchers can use is the shape of the rooms.
A cross-shaped church with the plan we see in Derinkuyu belongs to the Byzantine Christian world, so that part of the city must have been in use by then.
Comparisons with dated rock-cut churches and houses elsewhere in Cappadocia help a little more.
Beyond that, most dates you read for Derinkuyu are educated guesses.
Science can sometimes help where the rock cannot.
Where soot from lamps, charcoal from a hearth or seeds and bones survive in an undisturbed corner, radiocarbon dating can give a date for when they were left there.
But such deposits are rare in a city that has been cleared and reused so many times, and a date for a hearth tells you when someone lit a fire, not when the room around it was cut.
Every date has to be read with that in mind.
That uncertainty is not a failure.
It is the honest state of the evidence, and it is exactly where the myths rush in to fill the gap.
In the fourth century, three men from Cappadocia shaped Christian thought for the rest of history.
Basil, bishop of Caesarea, his younger brother Gregory of Nyssa, and their friend Gregory of Nazianzus are known together as the Cappadocian Fathers.
Their writings helped to settle the doctrine of the Trinity that most Christian churches still hold today.
Basil was also a practical man.
Outside Caesarea he built a great complex to care for the poor, the sick and travellers, which some historians count among the first hospitals.
And he wrote rules for monks living together in communities, rules that are still followed in Orthodox monasteries.
Monks found the valleys of Cappadocia ideal.
In the soft rock they could cut a cell, a chapel, a refectory with a table and benches carved out of the living stone.
Over the following centuries, hundreds of rock-cut churches appeared in the valleys around Göreme, Ihlara and Soğanlı.
Most of the painted churches that survive date from the ninth to the eleventh centuries.
The Tokalı church at Göreme, painted in the tenth century, is covered with scenes from the life of Christ in a deep blue that still glows.
The so-called Dark Church, which receives very little daylight, has kept its colours unusually fresh.
The paintings were not only decoration.
In a world where few people could read, they were how the stories of the faith were told.
The faces of saints, the scenes of Christ's birth and death, the warrior saints George and Theodore on horseback killing dragons, were all familiar to villagers who would never see Constantinople.
Many faces were later scratched out, and visitors from the last two centuries have carved their names over them.
These painted churches are the same world as the church deep inside Derinkuyu.
The same communities that carved chapels in the cliffs carved refuges under their villages.
One was for prayer in the open valleys.
The other was for the times when the open valleys were not safe.
And from the seventh century onwards, the times were very rarely safe.
Not everyone in Byzantine Cappadocia lived in a simple village.
Along the valleys there are rock-cut complexes of a quite different kind: great carved facades with arches and columns, opening onto courtyards, with halls, kitchens and stables behind them.

At Selime, at the end of the Ihlara valley, an entire cliff was hollowed out into a vast complex with a church, a huge hall with a high carved ceiling, and a kitchen with a chimney cut through the rock.

The art historian Veronica Kalas, who studied more than forty of these courtyard complexes, has argued that they were the houses of the local military aristocracy of the tenth and eleventh centuries, not monasteries as was long assumed.
These carved mansions show the other side of rock-cut life.
The rich could afford grand rooms in the cliffs, with decorated facades that faced the world.
The farmers in the villages, with fewer resources, dug down.
Both were making the most of the same rock, in the same centuries, under the same threats.
Even the birds were part of this carved economy.
All over Cappadocia, the cliffs are pierced with rows of small openings, often painted around the edges.
They are dovecotes, cut so that pigeons would nest in them.
The birds were valued less for their meat than for their droppings, which were collected and spread on the vineyards and orchards of the valleys, where the soil is poor.
Some of these dovecotes were still in use in the twentieth century.
It is a reminder that the underground cities were not built by a different people or a lost civilisation.
They were built by the same Byzantine Cappadocians whose churches, monasteries and houses fill the valleys above.
To understand Derinkuyu, you have to see it as part of that whole landscape, the bottom floor of a world carved into stone.
We are on firmer ground with the period when the city was used most.
From the seventh century AD, Cappadocia became a frontier.
To the south-east lay the new Islamic caliphate, to the west the Christian Byzantine Empire, and for roughly three centuries armies and raiding parties crossed this plateau again and again.
The raiders came through the passes of the Taurus Mountains, often in summer, seizing animals, crops and captives.
A farming village on an open plain could not hold out against them.
But a village that could vanish underground, with its animals, its grain and its water, could simply wait until the raiders moved on.
That is why most historians think the underground cities were greatly enlarged in the middle Byzantine period.
The Byzantine army itself recommended a similar answer.
When a large raiding army came, its commanders were told to avoid a pitched battle and to move the people of the countryside into strongholds, leaving the raiders little to take.
How close did the danger come?
In the summer of 806, the caliph Harun al-Rashid, famous today from the tales of the Thousand and One Nights, led one of the largest Abbasid invasions of Byzantine Anatolia.
His army came up through the Cilician Gates and reached Tyana, a city about sixty kilometres south of Derinkuyu, where he ordered a mosque to be built.
While the caliph besieged the fortress of Heraclea, part of his army was sent to plunder central Cappadocia.
Arab historians put that detachment at tens of thousands of men.
No source tells us what the villagers of Cappadocia did that summer.
But this is exactly the kind of raid the underground cities were made for.
The frontier left its mark on Byzantine literature too.

The epic of Digenis Akritis, the most famous poem of the Byzantine world, tells of a hero born of an Arab emir and a Byzantine noblewoman, who guards the borderlands of the east against raiders and bandits.
Its name means the two-blooded border lord.
It is a story, not a history, but it is set in exactly this world of raids, ambushes and frontier castles.
Thirty-two years later, in 838, another caliph, al-Mu'tasim, struck even harder.
One of his armies came up through the Cilician Gates and crossed Cappadocia to take Ancyra, modern Ankara.
Then the combined Abbasid forces besieged Amorium, the home city of the reigning Byzantine dynasty.
After about two weeks the city was taken and sacked, and thousands of its people were killed or carried off.
For the people of a Cappadocian village, campaigns like these were not distant news.
The armies marched through their fields.
When the frontier finally moved east in the tenth century, the danger did not end for good.
Later centuries would bring new invaders and new wars, and each time the cities underground could be opened and filled again.
In August 1071, near the town of Manzikert, far to the east, the Byzantine emperor Romanos the Fourth met the army of the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan.
The Byzantine army was defeated and the emperor himself was captured.
In the years of confusion that followed, Turkish groups spread across the Anatolian plateau, and Cappadocia passed out of Byzantine control.
A new state grew up on the plateau, the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, with its capital at Konya.
Its sultans built mosques, schools and, along the trade roads, great fortified inns for caravans.
One of the finest, the Sultanhanı near Aksaray, was built in 1229 on the road that runs west of Cappadocia.

Caravanserais like this were built along the main trade roads of the sultanate, roughly a day's travel apart, so that merchants, their animals and their goods could shelter behind high walls for the night.
Inside there was a courtyard, rooms, stables and often a small mosque.
The roads that the Assyrian merchants of Kanesh had used three thousand years earlier were busy again, and the sultans protected them because trade paid for their state.
The Christians of Cappadocia did not disappear.
Under the Seljuks and later under the Ottoman sultans, Christian villages survived across the region, side by side with Muslim ones.
Churches went on being cut and painted, more modestly than before.
In the valleys there are Greek inscriptions from the Seljuk period and later.
Under the Ottomans, who took over Cappadocia in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, the region became a quiet province of the empire, far from the great cities.
Villages were taxed, soldiers recruited, and roads maintained, but there were also long periods of insecurity, of bandits and local revolts.
The underground rooms beneath the villages, still known to the people who lived above them, kept their old purpose as stores and, when needed, as hiding places.
Many of these Christians gradually came to speak Turkish as their everyday language while keeping their Orthodox faith.
They are known as the Karamanlides.
They wrote Turkish in the Greek alphabet, and from the eighteenth century onwards printed whole books this way, Bibles, prayer books and newspapers, in a script that today almost no one can read.
In the nineteenth century, some of these villages grew rich.
Men went to work in Constantinople and sent money home, and their families built fine stone mansions.
At Sinasos, today Mustafapaşa, a few kilometres from Göreme, these houses still stand, with carved facades and painted ceilings.
And in many of these villages, under the houses, the old underground rooms were still there.
For most of its later history, the town above Derinkuyu was not called Derinkuyu at all.
Its Greek-speaking Christian inhabitants called it Malakopi.
Derinkuyu is Turkish and means deep well.
Cappadocia was home to a community of Orthodox Christians who spoke their own form of Greek, quite different from the Greek of Athens.
In the early twentieth century the British scholar Richard Dawkins travelled through their villages, Malakopi among them, and recorded their dialect before it disappeared.
How much the families of Malakopi still used the old passages is not well recorded.
The rooms nearest the surface may well have served as cellars and stores, as rock-cut rooms did all over Cappadocia, but the deep levels seem to have slipped out of everyday memory.
Then, in 1923, after the war between Greece and Turkey, the two countries agreed to exchange their populations.
Orthodox Christians in Turkey were sent to Greece, and Muslims in Greece were sent to Turkey.
More than a million people were moved.
The Christians of Malakopi left their homes, and with them went the memory of what lay underneath.
The agreement was signed at Lausanne, in Switzerland, on the thirtieth of January 1923.
It did not ask what language people spoke or how they saw themselves.
It asked only their religion.

So the Karamanlides of Cappadocia, Orthodox Christians whose everyday language was Turkish, were classed as Greeks and sent to Greece, a country many of them had never seen and whose language some of them barely spoke.
The villages emptied.
People were allowed to take only what they could carry.
Some carried their icons, some the keys of their houses.
In Greece, many refugee communities named their new villages after the old ones.
Families from Gelveri, today Güzelyurt, about thirty-five kilometres west of Derinkuyu, founded a new village in northern Greece and called it Nea Karvali, New Gelveri.
Muslim families arriving from Greece were settled in the houses they left behind.
In the space of a few years, the population of many Cappadocian towns was almost completely replaced.
The newcomers had no reason to know what the old cellars led to, and no one was left to tell them.
Forty years later, when a man knocked through his wall, the town above had new people who did not know the passages were there.
The city had to be discovered all over again.
After 1963, the people of Derinkuyu began clearing the passages they had found.
Rubble and earth that had filled rooms for generations were carried up to the surface, level by level.
A few years later, in 1969, the underground city was opened to visitors.
Today it is one of the most visited sites in Turkey.
Electric light and handrails have been added, and arrows mark the way down and the way back.
But only part of the city can be seen.
Many passages are closed, some because they are unsafe, others because they have never been fully cleared.
Clearing a place like this is slow, dangerous work.
Rooms were full of earth and fallen rock, and some passages had partly collapsed.
As each level was cleared, it had to be made safe before visitors could follow, and some parts were left closed.
One of the most repeated claims is that a tunnel joins Derinkuyu to Kaymaklı, about ten kilometres away.
A tunnel heading in that direction has been reported, but its full length has not been explored or published.
It may connect the two cities.
It may not.
Discoveries have not stopped.
In 2014, building work in the city of Nevşehir, about thirty kilometres to the north, broke into another network of tunnels and rooms beneath the old castle hill.
Its full extent is still being studied.
Cappadocia, it seems, has not yet shown us everything that lies beneath it.
Research continues.

In 2025, a study of the acoustics of Derinkuyu's deep shafts was presented to the Acoustical Society of America, and it is one of the sources for the figure of about fifty-five metres for the deepest well.
More than sixty years after the wall came down, the city is still being measured.
Tourism has changed the town above as well.
Coach parties arrive every morning, and the shops on the main street sell carpets and pottery.
Behind them, in ordinary courtyards, there are still doors that open onto stairs going down.
Derinkuyu has never really stopped being two towns, one above the other.
Ten kilometres north of Derinkuyu lies its nearest rival.
Kaymaklı was opened to visitors in 1964, a year after the discovery at Derinkuyu.
It does not go as deep, but it spreads out widely beneath the village, and only part of it can be visited.
What makes Kaymaklı remarkable is how closely it is tied to the village above.
Many houses in Kaymaklı still have doors in their cellars or courtyards that lead into the old tunnels, and people have used the upper rooms as storerooms and stables within living memory.
Here you can see how the underground city was simply the lowest floor of the village.
The rooms at Kaymaklı are low, the passages narrow and steep.
There are storerooms, niches, and stone blocks with hollows in them that guides call copper workings or kitchens; the identifications are not always certain.
There is even water trickling through the rock in places, a reminder of how damp and cold life below must have been.
Further north, near the town of Avanos, is Özkonak.
According to the local accounts, it came to light in 1972, when a villager irrigating his fields noticed that the water kept disappearing into the ground.
Following it, he found the tunnels beneath.
Özkonak has its own rolling stone doors and its own puzzles.
Small holes pierce the ceilings between some of its levels.
Guides say they were used to talk between floors, or even to pour hot liquid onto attackers below.
Both may be true.
Neither has been proven.
Most of these sites share the same features: narrow, winding passages; rolling stone doors; ventilation shafts; storerooms, stables and presses; and, often, a chapel.
It is like visiting different branches of the same family.
Each has its own character, but all of them were built for the same purpose, by people who faced the same dangers.

Derinkuyu, Kaymaklı and Özkonak are the three best known, but they are only the largest pieces of something much bigger: a whole region where, for more than a thousand years, every village kept a way down.
Derinkuyu is not unique.
Across the world, wherever people faced raiders they could not fight in the open, some of them went underground, and the solutions they found look strikingly alike.
In northern France, beneath the village of Naours in Picardy, there is a network of tunnels and rooms cut into the chalk.
Local people used it as a refuge during the wars of the seventeenth century, sheltering there with their animals.
In the First World War, soldiers from Britain, Australia and other countries visited the tunnels behind the front line, and left their names on the walls.
In southern Tunisia, at Matmata, Berber families still live in houses dug down into the ground: a deep circular pit open to the sky, with rooms cut into its sides.
Here the purpose was mostly not defence but climate.
Underground, the heat of the summer and the cold of winter nights are both kept out.
And then there are Xenophon's Armenian villages, which we met earlier.
People and animals sheltered together below ground through the winter, in houses reached by a narrow opening like a well.
Different places, different centuries, and the same two reasons: safety, and a steady temperature.
Closer to home, at Hattusa, the Hittites built a long stone tunnel under their walls, and other ancient peoples dug escape passages under their cities.
Medieval castles across Europe had cellars and sally ports.
But a refuge on the scale of a whole town, hidden beneath ordinary houses, is rare almost everywhere except here.
What makes Cappadocia special is the scale.
Nowhere else did so many communities, over so many centuries, carve so many refuges so deep.
That was possible because of the rock, and necessary because of the frontier.
Put the two together, and you get Derinkuyu.
There are many others besides the famous ones.
Underground settlements are known at Mazı, Tatlarin, Gaziemir and dozens of other villages, some only recently opened to visitors.
New entrances are still found, sometimes when a road is widened or a house is rebuilt.
Nobody knows how many remain undiscovered.
And the idea is not only ancient.
In the desert of South Australia lies the opal-mining town of Coober Pedy, where summer temperatures can climb above forty degrees.
Since the early twentieth century many of its people have lived in dugouts, homes carved into the hillsides, where the temperature stays comfortable all year.
There are underground houses, shops and churches.
It is a modern town that solved the old problem in the same old way.
Now we can return to the claims we started with.
Eighteen levels?
No published survey supports it.
At least eight levels are known, and the official figure for the open part of the city is eight.
More may lie below, but eighteen is a number that has been repeated, not measured.
Twenty thousand people?
That figure appears in newspapers and travel guides, but none of them names the researcher who calculated it.
The city was large enough to shelter many families with their animals.
How many, no one has shown.
The honest statement is that estimates run as high as twenty thousand.
Xenophon?
He described underground houses in Armenia, not Cappadocia.
And the claims that giants, a lost civilisation or visitors from elsewhere carved it have no evidence behind them at all.
Everything about Derinkuyu, from its tool marks to its church, points to ordinary people, working with simple tools, over a very long time.
And the tunnel to Kaymaklı?
Reported, but not mapped or published from end to end.
The church and the rolling doors?
Real, and you can see them.
The fifty-five-metre well?
Reported in recent research.
The Phrygians?
Possible, not proven.
The Byzantine refuges from the Arab raids?
The best supported part of the whole story.
Sorting the claims like this does not make Derinkuyu smaller.
It shows which parts of the story stand on solid rock.
Which leaves the real answers to our three questions.
How was it built?
By hand, in a soft rock that its builders understood perfectly, one room at a time.
Who built it?
Many generations of Cappadocians, whose names are lost, ending with the Christian villagers of Malakopi.
And why?
Because for centuries this plateau was a frontier, and the safest place to be was underground.
There is one more thing worth saying.
The real story is better than the myths.
A city dug by giants or aliens would be a curiosity.

A city dug by farmers, with iron picks, by lamplight, over centuries, to keep their children and their animals alive while armies marched over their heads, is something else: one of the great achievements of ordinary people anywhere in the ancient and medieval world.
Questions remain, and some of them may one day be answered.
How deep does the city really go, below the levels open to visitors?
Is there a tunnel to Kaymaklı, and how long is it?
When were the first rooms cut?
Careful survey, new dating methods and the study of the other underground settlements of Cappadocia may give better answers than we have now.
For the moment, the honest position is to enjoy the mystery that is real, and leave aside the ones that were invented.
Walk back up the stairs and out into the daylight, and the town looks ordinary again: houses, a mosque, a main street.
Under your feet, eighty-five metres of rock are still hollow, a reminder that for a very long time the people of Cappadocia survived by hiding.
And they hid so well that their hiding place was almost forgotten.
